lead: A practical source has internal resistance, so its terminal voltage sags as the load draws more current. Two circuits reproduce that sag exactly: a voltage source in series with a resistor, and a current source in parallel with the same resistor. Swapping one for the other, with Is = Vs/R, is source transformation (some syllabi call it source conversion). It lets you merge sources, prepare a circuit for mesh or nodal analysis, and it is the step behind the Thevenin and Norton equivalents of the network theorems.
prereq: You need: practical sources from Independent and dependent sources, and the current divider from Series-parallel circuits.

sections.h3: Two models, one pair of terminals

blocks.text: Voltage form: an ideal Vs in series with R. KVL gives the terminal voltage v = Vs − iR, where i is the current delivered to the load.
Current form: an ideal Is in parallel with R. KCL at the top terminal gives i = Is − v/R; multiply by R and rearrange: v = IsR − iR.

The two lines are identical when Vs = IsR. Then both forms have the same open-circuit voltage Vs, the same short-circuit current Is and the same terminal line between them, so no load connected to the two terminals can tell them apart. Only the inside differs.
Is = Vs/R (voltage form to current form) and Vs = IsR (current form to voltage form). R keeps its value; it moves from series to parallel or back.

items: Find a practical source: an ideal voltage source with a resistor in series, or an ideal current source with a resistor in parallel.
Compute the new source value; keep R.
Set the direction: the current arrow points towards the terminal that was the + terminal of the voltage source. Going back, the + terminal goes on the side the arrow points to.
Redraw, then merge with neighbouring elements and continue reducing.

blocks.text: The direction rule follows from the short-circuit current: shorting the voltage form drives current out of its + terminal and round through the short, so the current source must push current out of the same terminal. Only practical sources transform. An ideal voltage source (no series R) and an ideal current source (no parallel R) have no equivalent in the other form.

items: Voltage sources in series add with their signs: aiding sources add, opposing sources subtract. Their series resistors add.
Current sources in parallel add with their signs: arrows the same way add, opposite arrows subtract. Their parallel resistors combine in parallel.
So to merge practical sources in parallel, convert each to the current form, add; to merge practical sources in series, convert each to the voltage form, add.
A dependent source with its resistor transforms in the same way (I = μv<sub>x</sub>/R, for example), provided the control variable is not inside the part being transformed.
The load stays outside the transformation; the equivalence holds only at the two kept terminals. Terminal voltage and current carry over, but the power inside the source model does not.

figure.caption: The second worked example in three steps: each practical voltage source becomes a current source (12/3 = 4 A, 18/6 = 3 A), the two current sources and the two resistors merge, and the result goes back to a 14 V source with 2 Ω in series.

spec.aria: Panel a: a 12 V source with 3 ohm and an 18 V source with 6 ohm in parallel across a 2 ohm load. Panel b: one 7 A current source, 2 ohm and the load in parallel. Panel c: a 14 V source with 2 ohm in series and the 2 ohm load, carrying 3.5 A at 7 V.

examples.question: A 24 V source with 6 Ω in series feeds a 3 Ω load. (a) Find the load current and voltage directly. (b) Transform the source and find them again. (c) Compare the power delivered by the ideal source in each model.
steps: (a) The 6 Ω and the 3 Ω are in series: I = 24/(6 + 3) = 24/9 = 2.667 A; load voltage V = 2.667 × 3 = 8 V.
(b) Transform: I<sub>s</sub> = 24/6 = 4 A, in parallel with 6 Ω, arrow pointing to the terminal that was +.
The 6 Ω and the 3 Ω load are now in parallel across the 4 A source. Current divider: load current = 4 × 6/(6 + 3) = 2.667 A; V = 2.667 × 3 = 8 V. Same as (a).
(c) Voltage form: the 24 V source delivers 24 × 2.667 = 64 W. Current form: the 4 A source has 8 V across it and delivers 8 × 4 = 32 W. The load takes 8 × 2.667 = 21.33 W in both.
examples.answer: 2.667 A and 8 V in both models; the ideal sources deliver 64 W and 32 W, so internal power does not carry over.

examples.question: Two practical sources share a 2 Ω load, all three in parallel: 12 V with 3 Ω in series, and 18 V with 6 Ω in series, both with + at the top. Use source transformation to find the load current and voltage, then check each source's current.
steps: Transform each source: 12/3 = 4 A in parallel with 3 Ω; 18/6 = 3 A in parallel with 6 Ω; both arrows point up, to the top wire.
Merge: currents in parallel and the same way add, 4 + 3 = 7 A. Resistors in parallel: 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2 Ω.
Transform back: 7 A × 2 Ω = 14 V in series with 2 Ω, + at the top.
With the 2 Ω load: I = 14/(2 + 2) = 3.5 A, and V = 3.5 × 2 = 7 V.
Check in the original circuit, top wire at 7 V: the 12 V source sends (12 − 7)/3 = 1.667 A and the 18 V source sends (18 − 7)/6 = 1.833 A. KCL: 1.667 + 1.833 = 3.5 A.
examples.answer: Load current 3.5 A at 7 V; the sources supply 1.667 A and 1.833 A.

traps: Reversing the current arrow. It points to the terminal that was +; flip it and every later current changes sign.
Transforming an ideal source. Without a series R (voltage) or a parallel R (current) there is nothing to transform.
Keeping R in both places. The series R moves to parallel; it is the same resistor, not a second one.
Swallowing the load into the transformation. Keep the element whose current you want outside.
Comparing internal powers. In the first example the ideal sources deliver 64 W and 32 W, yet the load takes 21.33 W either way.

quiz.q: State the source transformation rule for V<sub>s</sub> in series with R, including the arrow.
quiz.a: It becomes I<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/R in parallel with the same R, the arrow pointing to the terminal that was the + terminal of V<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Why do the two models give the same terminal current for every load?
quiz.a: Both obey v = V<sub>s</sub> − iR when V<sub>s</sub> = I<sub>s</sub>R. One terminal line means one operating point with any load.

quiz.q: Convert 12 V in series with 4 Ω, and 4 A in parallel with 2 Ω.
quiz.a: 12/4 = 3 A in parallel with 4 Ω, arrow to the old + terminal. 4 × 2 = 8 V in series with 2 Ω, + on the side the arrow pointed to.

quiz.q: Two practical voltage sources are in series and aiding: 10 V with 1 Ω and 5 V with 4 Ω. They feed a 5 Ω load. Find the load current.
quiz.a: Series sources add: 10 + 5 = 15 V with 1 + 4 = 5 Ω. Load current = 15/(5 + 5) = 1.5 A.

quiz.q: Current sources of 3 A and 2 A, with 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel, feed the same node pair. Find the merged source if the arrows agree, and if they oppose.
quiz.a: Agreeing: 3 + 2 = 5 A, opposing: 3 − 2 = 1 A in the direction of the 3 A source. Either way R = 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω. Voltage forms: 10 V or 2 V in series with 2 Ω.

quiz.q: A 10 V source with 5 Ω in series feeds a 10 Ω load. Transform it and show the load power is unchanged but the ideal source's power is not.
quiz.a: Voltage form: I = 10/15 = 0.667 A, load voltage 6.667 V, load power 4.444 W; the source delivers 10 × 0.667 = 6.667 W. Current form: 2 A ∥ 5 Ω; 5 ∥ 10 = 3.333 Ω, V = 6.667 V, load current 0.667 A, load power 4.444 W; the source delivers 2 × 6.667 = 13.33 W.

beyond: Not for the exam. Nodal-analysis programs fold each voltage source that has a series resistance into a current source and a conductance, and keep ideal voltage sources as extra unknowns (modified nodal analysis). Battery datasheets quote internal resistance so that the practical model can predict sag under load. The same equivalence grows into the Thevenin and Norton theorems. Search next for Norton equivalents and modified nodal analysis.
